certainty_reasoning: Facts first: the editors state that four Wilde-to-Pollitt letters survive and that Wilde misspelt his name in all four (p. 1120 n. 2); no letter from Pollitt to Wilde is printed in this edition, so only one side of the exchange exists in the record. The two men appear never to have met during the correspondence: on 3 December 1898 Wilde takes the colour of Pollitt's hair on Ada Leverson's authority and says of a photograph 'not a bit like you, I am sure' (pp. 1106-1107), and on 3 January 1899, having received two dissimilar photographs, he is still asking their mutual publisher Leonard Smithers 'What is he like?' (p. 1117). Direction: Wilde's, and the anchor is his first letter - the request for a photograph is made by Wilde, unprompted, on 26 November 1898 (p. 1103), before any photograph is sent. Outcome: unknown - Pollitt answered, sent at least four photographs, signed himself 'Jerome', kept the letters (now MS Princeton) and accepted inscribed presentation copies of the French Ballad of Reading Gaol and The Importance of Being Earnest, which is real reciprocity of a kind; but with no Pollitt text in evidence nothing shows what he understood himself to be answering, and no meeting is recorded.
date_label: Four surviving letters, 26 November 1898 to 19 January 1899, all from Wilde in exile (Hotel d'Alsace, Paris, then Hotel des Bains, Napoule): [postmark 26 November 1898] p. 1103; 3 December 1898 pp. 1106-1107; [postmark of receipt 31 December 1898] pp. 1115-1116; [postmark 19 January 1899] p. 1120. The General Index also lists an unannotated mention at printed 1103. No meeting is recorded at any point.
summary: Between November 1898 and January 1899 Wilde wrote four surviving letters to Herbert Charles Pollitt - 'Jerome' to his friends, a Kendal-born Cambridge man who had danced ballet as an amateur undergraduate and collected Beardsley drawings from Wilde's own publisher. Wilde opened the correspondence by asking outright for a photograph of him; Pollitt sent two, then more, and Wilde spent much of the remaining three letters comparing them, preferring the one in the Norfolk suit, dismissing a Hollyer portrait as unlike him, and pronouncing a later one in a Coan robe - the editors gloss the word as transparent - most becoming. He carried the Norfolk-suit photograph with him to the Riviera and told Pollitt he looked for him daily. The two never met: as late as January 1899, holding two photographs that did not resemble each other, Wilde was reduced to asking Leonard Smithers what Pollitt was actually like. In the last of the letters Wilde teased him about the spelling of his own name; the editors note drily that it was Wilde who had it wrong, in all four.

sources.quote: Wilde spelt it wrong in all the four surviving letters (see note 1, p.1116).

sources.quote: How is Pollitt? He has sent me two photographs of himself: in one he is fair, in the other dark; and neither resembles the other. What _is_ he like?
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, [postmark 3 January 1899], Hotel des Bains, Napoule; the closing lines of the letter, immediately before 'Ever yours OSCAR'. Heading as printed: 'To Leonard Smithers / MS Princeton'. 'is' underlined in the original.
sources.supports: The class-deciding fact: five weeks into the correspondence and holding two photographs, Wilde still had to ask a third party what Pollitt looked like - the two had not met

sources.quote: Dear Mr Pollitt, I should like a photograph of you, of all things. Pray let me have one.
sources.context: Wilde to H. C. Pollitt, [postmark 26 November 1898], Hotel d'Alsace [Paris]; the opening of the first of the four surviving letters. Heading as printed: 'To H. C. Pollitt / MS Princeton'. Signed 'Sincerely yours OSCAR WILDE'. The rest of the letter concerns customs duty on photographs, the forthcoming Importance of Being Earnest, Wilde's shortage of money, and a joke on the name Jerome and St Jerome's lion.

sources.quote: Pollitt's Kendal home was called The Green Window.

sources.quote: Dear Mr Pollitt, Thank you so much for the two photographs you have so kindly sent me. I like the little one, in the Norfolk suit, best: it looks young and nice: the other, the one by Hollyer, looks to me like the portrait of an Oxford Dean – troubled and affected and ineffectual: not a bit like you, I am sure. Mrs Leverson, a recognised authority for the colour of young men's hair, assured me you were quite golden, and I have always thought of you as a sort of gilt sunbeam masquerading in clothes, but, no doubt, you are Protean, and have many forms. When you come to Paris pray be golden entirely, and leave your more serious aspect in charge of Smithers, who needs, indeed, some stern monitor for his manner of living.
sources.context: Wilde to H. C. Pollitt, 3 December 1898, Paris - the opening of the letter, answering two photographs Pollitt had sent.
sources.supports: The sustained request-and-comment pattern on which the direction rests; the passages are the flirtatious core of the correspondence
sources.citation_provenance: PDF pp. 1152-1153; the editors' footnote marker after 'Hollyer' is dropped.

sources.quote: … assured me you were quite golden, and I have always thought of you as a sort of gilt sunbeam masquerading in clothes, but, no doubt, you are Protean, and have many forms. When you come to Paris pray be golden entirely, and leave your more serious aspect in charge of Smithers, who needs, indeed, some stern monitor for his manner of living. No: don't come to the Hôtel d'Alsace; it is a poor little Bohemian hotel, only suited for those Sybarites who are exiled from Sybaris. It would be a poor background for you, and background is so much. Go to some purple place, which will go with your hair: and bring a green window with you that you may look out on life in proper fashion: attitude is all. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to H. C. Pollitt, Paris, December 1898 - the close of the letter; it begins on the preceding folio and the quote starts where this page does, mid-sentence. The editors note that Pollitt's Kendal home was called The Green Window, which is the joke in the last sentence. The same folio carries the letter to Turner that names Alphonse, Joseph and Hylton's boy Herbert.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde on Pollitt's goldness, and telling him where not to stay.
